translation.text:
NORA. Tomorrow I am going home— I mean, to my old hometown. It will be easiest for me there to find my way into something or other.

HELMER. Oh, you blind, inexperienced creature.

NORA. I must try to gain experience, Torvald.

HELMER. Leave your home, your husband, and your children! And you do not think about what people will say.

NORA. I cannot take that into consideration. I only know that it will be necessary for me.

HELMER. Oh, it is outrageous. That you can betray your most sacred duties in this way.

NORA. What, then, do you consider my most sacred duties?

HELMER. And should I have to tell you that! Are they not your duties toward your husband and your children?

NORA. I have other, equally sacred duties.

HELMER. You do not. What duties could those be?

NORA. My duties toward myself.

HELMER. First and foremost, you are a wife and mother.

NORA. I no longer believe that. I believe that first and foremost I am a human being, I, just as much as you are—or at any rate that I shall try to become one. I know very well that most people agree with you, Torvald, and that something of the sort is written in the books. But I can no longer content myself with what most people say and what is written in the books. I must think those things over for myself and try to understand them.

HELMER. Should you not understand your position in your own home? Do you not have an infallible guide in such matters? Do you not have religion?

NORA. Oh, Torvald, I really do not properly know what religion is at all.

HELMER. What are you saying!

NORA. I know nothing except what Pastor Hansen said when I was preparing for confirmation. He told us that religion was this and that. When I get away from all this here and am alone, I shall investigate that matter too. I shall see whether what Pastor Hansen said was right, or at any rate whether it is right for me.

HELMER. Oh, such a thing is really unheard of from so young a woman! But if religion cannot guide you, then at least let me stir your conscience. You do have moral feeling, surely? Or answer me—perhaps you have none?

NORA. Well, Torvald, that is not easy to answer. I really do not know at all. I am completely at a loss about those things. I only know that I have an entirely different opinion about such matters from you. I now also hear that the laws are different from what I thought; but that those laws should be right is something I simply cannot get into my head. So a woman is not to have the right to spare her old, dying father, or to save her husband’s life! I do not believe in such things.

HELMER. You speak like a child. You do not understand the society in which you live.

NORA. No, I do not. But now I shall acquaint myself with it. I must try to find out who is right, society or I.

HELMER. You are ill, Nora; you have a fever; I almost think you are out of your senses.

NORA. I have never felt so clear and certain as I do tonight.

HELMER. And clear and certain, you leave your husband and your children?

NORA. Yes; I do.

HELMER. Then only one explanation is possible.

NORA. Which one?

HELMER. You do not love me anymore.

NORA. No, that is precisely it.

HELMER. Nora!—And you say that!

NORA. Oh, it hurts me so much, Torvald; for you have always been so kind to me. But I cannot help it. I do not love you anymore.

HELMER (with hard-won composure). Is this too a clear and certain conviction?

NORA. Yes, perfectly clear and certain. That is why I do not want to be here any longer.

HELMER. And will you also be able to explain to me how I have forfeited your love?

NORA. Yes, I can easily do that. It was this evening, when the wonderful thing did not happen; for then I saw that you were not the man I had imagined you to be.

HELMER. Explain yourself more precisely; I do not understand you.

NORA. I have waited so patiently for eight years now; for, good Lord, I understood well enough that the wonderful thing does not happen like that every day. Then this crushing blow broke over me; and then I was so unshakably certain: now the wonderful thing will happen. When Krogstad’s letter was lying out there, it never entered my mind for an instant that you might be willing to submit to that man’s terms. I was so unshakably certain that you would say to him: make the matter known to the whole world. And when that had happened—

HELMER. Yes, what then? When I had surrendered my own wife to shame and disgrace—!

NORA. When that had happened, I thought with such unshakable certainty that you would step forward, take everything upon yourself, and say: I am the guilty one.

HELMER. Nora—!

NORA. You think that I would never have accepted such a sacrifice from you? No, of course not. But what would my assurances have counted for against yours?—That was the wonderful thing for which I went on hoping in terror. And it was to prevent it that I wanted to end my life.

HELMER. I would gladly work nights and days for you, Nora—bear sorrow and privation for your sake. But no one sacrifices his honor for the one he loves.

NORA. A hundred thousand women have done so.

HELMER. Oh, you both think and speak like an unreasonable child.

NORA. So be it. But you neither think nor speak like the man with whom I could unite myself. When your terror was over—not at what threatened me, but at what you yourself were exposed to—and when all the danger was past, then for you it was as though absolutely nothing had happened. I was exactly as before, your little song-lark, your doll, whom you would henceforth carry doubly carefully in your hands, since it was so fragile and frail. (Rises.) Torvald—in that moment it dawned on me that for eight years I had lived here with a strange man, and that I had borne three children—. Oh, I cannot bear to think of it! I could tear myself into bits and pieces.

HELMER (heavily). I see it; I see it. An abyss has surely opened between us.—Oh, but Nora, could it not be filled in?

NORA. As I am now, I am no wife for you.

HELMER. I have the strength to become another man.

NORA. Perhaps—if your doll is taken away from you.

HELMER. Oh, to part—to part from you! No, no, Nora, I cannot grasp that thought.

NORA (goes into the room on the right). All the more certainly must it happen. (She returns with her outer garments and a small traveling bag, which she places on the chair by the table.)

HELMER. Nora, Nora, not now! Wait until tomorrow.

NORA (puts on her coat). I cannot spend the night in a strange man’s rooms.

HELMER. But could we not live here as brother and sister—?

NORA. Only to sew on my costume. Good heavens, how unreasonable you are.
(sits down on the sofa.) Now be good, Doctor Rank; tomorrow you shall
see how beautifully I shall dance; and then you must imagine that I am
doing it only for your sake—yes, and then, of course, for
Torvald’s—that goes without saying. (takes various things out of the box.)
Doctor Rank, sit down here, and I shall show you something.

RANK (sits down). What is it?

NORA. Look here. Look!

RANK. Silk stockings.

NORA. Flesh-colored. Aren’t they lovely? Yes, it is so dark
in here now; but tomorrow—. No, no, no; you may only see the foot. Oh
well, you may indeed see the upper part too, if you like.

RANK. Hm—

NORA. Why do you look so critical? Perhaps you don’t think
they will fit?

RANK. I cannot possibly have any well-founded opinion about
that.

NORA (looks at him for a moment). Shame on you. (taps him lightly
on the ear with the stockings.) That is what you get. (packs them up again.)

RANK. And what other delights am I to be allowed to see?

NORA. You will not be allowed to see another bit; for you
are naughty.

(she hums a little and searches among the things.)

RANK (after a brief silence). When I sit here like this,
quite intimately together with you, I cannot understand—no, I cannot
comprehend—what would have become of me if I had never come into this
house.

NORA (smiles). Oh, I think you are actually quite comfortable
with us.

RANK (more softly, staring ahead). And then to have to leave
all of it—

NORA. Nonsense; you are not leaving it.

RANK (as before). —and not even be able to leave behind one
poor token of gratitude; scarcely even a fleeting sense of loss—nothing
but an empty place that can be filled by the first person who comes along.

NORA. And if I were now to ask you to—? No—

RANK. To what?

NORA. For a great proof of your friendship—

RANK. Yes, yes?

NORA. No, I mean—for an immensely great service—

RANK. Would you really, for once, make me so happy?

NORA. Oh, you do not know at all what it is.

RANK. Very well, then; say it.

NORA. No, but I cannot, Doctor Rank; it is something so
unreasonably great—advice and help and a service, all at once—

RANK. So much the better. I cannot imagine what you can
mean. But do speak. Do I not have your confidence?

NORA. Yes, you do, as no one else does. You are my most
faithful and best friend; you know that well enough. That is why I will
tell you. Very well, then, Doctor Rank; there is something you must help
me prevent. You know how deeply, how indescribably dearly Torvald loves
me; never for a moment would he hesitate to give his life for my sake.

RANK (leaning toward her). Nora—do you think, then, that he
is the only one—?

NORA (with a slight start). Who—?

RANK. Who would gladly give his life for your sake.

NORA (heavily). I see.

RANK. I swore to myself that you should know it before I
went away. I would never find a better opportunity. Yes, Nora, now you
know it. And now you also know that you can confide in me as in no one
else.

NORA (rises; evenly and calmly). Let me pass.

RANK (makes room for her but remains seated). Nora—

NORA (in the doorway to the hall). Helen, bring in the lamp.
—(goes over toward the stove.) Oh, dear Doctor Rank, that was really
horrid of you.

RANK (rises). That I have loved you every bit as deeply as
anyone else has? Was that horrid?

NORA. No, but that you should go and tell me. There was no
need at all—

RANK. What do you mean? Did you know, then—?

(The maid enters with the lamp, puts it on the table, and goes out again.)

RANK. Nora—Mrs. Helmer—I ask you, did you know anything?

NORA. Oh, how do I know what I knew or did not know? I
really cannot tell you—. How could you be so clumsy, Doctor Rank!
Everything was so good as it was.

RANK. Well, at any rate, you now know for certain that I am
at your disposal, body and soul. And will you speak freely now?

NORA (looks at him). After this?

RANK. I beg you, let me know what it is.

NORA. You cannot be told anything now.

RANK. Yes, yes. You must not punish me like this. Let me be
allowed to do for you whatever lies within human power.

NORA. Now you can do nothing for me. Besides, I am sure I
do not need any help. You will see that it is all merely imagination.
Yes, surely that is so. Of course! (sits down in the rocking chair,
looks at him, smiles.) Well, you certainly are a fine gentleman, Doctor
Rank. Don’t you think you ought to be ashamed of yourself now that the
lamp has come in?

RANK. No; not really. But perhaps I should go—for good?

NORA. No, you certainly must not do that. Naturally, you
must come here as before. You know very well that Torvald cannot do
without you.

RANK. Yes, but you?

NORA. Oh, I always think it becomes tremendously pleasant
here when you come.

RANK. That is precisely what led me astray. You are a riddle
to me. Many a time it has seemed to me that you would almost as soon be
with me as with Helmer.

NORA. Yes, you see, there are some people whom one loves
most, and other people whom one would almost rather be with.

RANK. Ah yes, there is something in that.

NORA. When I was at home, I naturally loved Papa most. But
I always thought it was so immensely amusing when I could steal down to
the maids’ room; for they did not lecture me in the least, and they
always talked so amusingly among themselves.

RANK. Aha; so it is they whom I have replaced.

NORA (springs up and goes over to him). Oh, dear, kind Doctor
Rank, that is not at all what I meant. But surely you can understand
that with Torvald it is just as it was with Papa—

(The maid enters from the hall.)

MAID. Madam! (whispers and hands her a card.)

NORA (glances at the card). Ah! (puts it in her pocket.)

RANK. Is something wrong?

NORA. No, no, not at all; it is only something—it is my new
costume—

RANK. What do you mean? Your costume is lying right there.

NORA. Oh yes, that one; but there is another; I have ordered
it—Torvald must not know about it—

RANK. Aha, so there we have the great secret.

NORA. Yes, indeed; just go in to him; he is sitting in the
inner room; keep him occupied for a while—

RANK. Do not worry; he shall not get away from me. (he goes
into Helmer’s room.)

NORA (to the maid). And he is standing waiting in the kitchen?

MAID. Yes, he came up the back stairs—

NORA. But did you not tell him that someone was here?

MAID. Yes, but it did no good.

NORA. He will not go away again?

MAID. No, he will not go until he has spoken with Madam.

And now she began to speak, eager to win him back. She said that
it had not been her intention to abandon him forever, but that for
a time, for appearance’s sake, they had to break off their relationship.
He had been able to see for himself that her father stood on the
threshold of madness, that her mother’s life was in constant danger.
Surely he must understand that she had been compelled to go home.

Then his anger burst forth in words. She need not pretend. He
no longer wished to be her plaything. She had abandoned him as soon
as she had been able to go home, and he could not love her anymore.
When he had come home from the hunt the day before yesterday and found
her gone without a greeting, without a word, his blood had frozen in
his veins; he had nearly died of grief. He could not love the woman
who had caused him such great pain. Besides, she had never loved him.
She was a coquette who wanted someone to kiss and caress her here in
her home district as well; that was all.

Did he think, then, that she was in the habit of letting young
gentlemen caress her?

Oh yes, he certainly did. Women were not as holy as they looked.
Selfishness and coquetry from beginning to end! No, if only she had
known how he had felt when he came home from the hunt! It was as though
he had been wading through ice water. He would never overcome that
pain. It would follow him throughout his life. He could never be a
human being again.

She tried to explain to him how everything had happened. She
sought to remind him that she was still faithful.

Yes, it made no difference, for now he no longer loved her. Now
he had seen through her. She was selfish. She did not love him. She
had left without giving him a greeting.

Incessantly he returned to this. She almost enjoyed the scene.
She could not become angry. She understood his anger so well. Nor
did she fear any real rupture. In the end, however, she grew uneasy.
Had such a change truly taken place in him that he could no longer
care for her?

“Gösta!” she said. “Was I selfish when I went to Sjö for the
Major? I did remember that they had smallpox there. Nor is it pleasant
to walk outdoors in thin shoes in cold and snow.”

“Love lives on love, not on services and good deeds,” said Gösta.

“Then you want us to be strangers from now on, Gösta?”

“That is what I want.”

“Gösta Berling is very changeable.”

“I am commonly accused of such things.”

He was cold, impossible to warm, and in truth she herself was
colder still. Self-observation sat sneering at her attempts to play
the woman in love.

“Gösta!” she said, making one more effort. “I have never
intentionally wronged you, though it may look that way. I beg you:
forgive me!”

“I cannot forgive you.”

She knew that if she had possessed one whole, genuine feeling,
she would have won him back. And she tried to act passionate. The
eyes of ice mocked her, but she tried all the same. She did not want
to lose him.

“Do not go, Gösta! Do not go in anger! Think how ugly I have
become! No one can love me anymore.”

“Nor do I,” he said. “You must resign yourself to seeing your
heart trampled underfoot, as others do.”

“Gösta, I have never been able to love anyone but you. Forgive
me! Do not abandon me! You are the only one who can save me from
myself.”

He pushed her away.

“You are not telling the truth,” he said with icy calm. “I do
not know what you want of me, but I see that you are lying. Why do
you want to keep me? You are so rich that you will never lack
suitors.”

With that, he left.

And no sooner had he closed the door than longing and pain, in
all their majesty, made their entrance into Marianne’s heart.

It was Love, the child of her own heart, who came forth from the
corner to which the eyes of ice had banished him. He came, the longed-for
one, now, when it was too late. Now he stepped forth, solemn and
almighty, and longing and pain bore up his royal mantle.

When Marianne could tell herself with true certainty that Gösta
Berling had abandoned her, she experienced an almost physical pain,
so terrible that she was nearly stupefied. She pressed her hands to
her heart and sat for hours in the same place, struggling with tearless
grief.

And it was she herself who suffered, not a stranger, not an
actress. It was she herself.

Why had her father come and torn them apart? Her love had not
been dead. It was only in her weakened condition after her illness
that she had been unable to feel his power.

O God, O God, that she had lost him! O God, that she had awakened
so late!

Ah, he was the only one, he was the master of her heart! From
him she could endure anything. Harshness and cruel words from him
only bowed her into humble love. If he had struck her, she would have
crawled to him like a dog and kissed his hand.

She snatched up pen and paper and wrote with terrible eagerness.
First she wrote of her love and longing. Then she begged, not for his
love, only for his mercy. It was some kind of verse that she wrote.

She did not know what to do to obtain relief from this dull pain.

When she had finished, she thought that if he were to see this,
he would at least believe that she loved him. Well, why should she
not send what she had written to him? The next day she would send it
off, and she fully believed that it would bring him back to her.

The next day she went about in anguish and conflict with herself.
What she had written seemed so pitiful and foolish to her. It had
neither rhyme nor meter. It was only prose. Surely he would only
laugh at such verses.

Her pride awakened as well. If he no longer loved her, then it
was such a dreadful humiliation to beg for his love.

At times prudence came and told her that she ought to be glad
that she had escaped from her relationship with Gösta and all the
distressing circumstances it would bring with it.

The torments of her heart were so terrible, however, that in the
end her feelings were allowed to rule. Three days after the day on
which she had become conscious of her love, she had placed the verses
in an envelope and written Gösta Berling’s name on the cover. Yet
they were not sent. Before she had found a suitable messenger, she
had heard such things about Gösta Berling that she realized it was
already too late to win him back.

“I remember,” he began, “a day in the month of March, when you came to see me at my house for the first time. I was asleep. You were almost a child then, or seemed to be, and you showed me a gold bracelet. Yes!... and now I no longer have that house, or at least I must leave it, because there has been a scandal and people avoid greeting me... Do you know? It means that you will have a house, and one more beautiful and richer than mine, since Rafa spends freely. Provided, however, that you do not grow too fat... Rafa, I warn you, abhors women who are too fat. Then I also remember an outing we took together, on the shores of a certain lake... But it was for one night only; perhaps you have lost the memory of it amid so many things.

He watched her, questioned her, intimidated her with his sinister eyes.

“Tell me a little about your life, then!... Have you no voice left?”

His sister asked in a firm, simple tone:

“Why have you come?”

He stared at her for a moment, his eyes gleaming brightly:

“I was passing by,” he replied; “the wall is not high; I felt like paying you a visit.”

“Why have you come?” she repeated once more, in a deeper voice.

“Ah!... Perhaps you thought you would never see me again? Had you already put your heart at peace?”

A wicked and somber anger fleetingly appeared in her, as it did on her brother’s face.

“I have done you no harm,” she said sharply, with complete certainty.

“You?”

“No harm,” she reiterated, more sharply still.

He sprang to his feet, livid, as if to seize her.

“No, do not touch me!” she commanded, shielding herself with both arms. “If you had wanted me, I was yours; you could freely have done with me whatever you pleased... Do not forget it!”

“What are you saying?” he murmured, surprised by these words, struck full force by this truth.

“When I was, as you said, a child, when I came to your house for the first time, and afterward, and always, until the day you fled, you could have done with me whatever you pleased. I would never have taken revenge or complained.”

She too paused, since he was silent, overcome with astonishment.

“But now what are you asking of me?” Loretta added.

“What am I asking of you?... A little clarification, a matter of no consequence: for what reason did you become Rafa’s mistress?”

She turned her eyes irresolutely elsewhere, toward the motionless trees, toward the restless stars, toward the luminous shadow of the cerulean night.

“Answer!”

“I do not know.”

“For love?”

“No.”

“For money?”

“Not that either.”

“Did he perhaps take you by force?”

“No.”

“Then why?”

“I do not know, I do not know!...” she said nervously. “Why do you want to torment me?”

“Answer: did you love him? Do you love him?”

“No. I said no.”

She sensed that these words would save her, and repeated once more:

“Neither before nor now; I do not love him.”

And what was more, it was indeed true.

A kind of vertigo passed through the eyes of the man staring at her; a trace, almost already a smile, almost a kiss, rippled across his bitter mouth.

“Then why did you do this?”

“I myself could not tell you,” his sister confessed. “It was madness, a moment of thoughtlessness, something unforeseen and easy, without gravity yet almost necessary... One day I did it, and I cannot even tell you the reason. Perhaps because you had tormented me so much, perhaps because I made the mistake of going up a staircase... I do not know, I do not know!”

And now she was no longer afraid of him; she spoke to him almost gently, her lovely color returning to her blooming cheeks, passing a ringed hand over her white temple and smoothing her hair with a habitual gesture of hers.

“And I?” her brother murmured after remaining silent.

“You?”

“Yes, Lora, I, who loved you with such anguish, I, who fled desperately so as not to hurt you?...”

She hesitated a little, then said:

“You did not want me... you did not want me even when I wept over it, and so...”

In the terrible simplicity of these words she gathered together the entire logic of her little woman’s heart; she solved her little feminine enigma, in which the maddest love had, at bottom, been nothing but a murky curiosity. She could go no further; the whole story of her great sin ended in this small reflection: “You did not want me, and so...”

And he lowered his face, then began rapping his knuckles on the little wicker table, which rocked.

“So,” he said, bitterly and mockingly, “you simply needed someone to lay you down forcefully, with your shoulders upon a cushion, someone to make you finally utter that little cry... Who that person was mattered little. I had tormented you greatly... did you say tormented?... very well, so be it! But in any case you chose a rich man, to sweeten the pains of martyrdom; in exchange you wanted a few dresses, a few jewels, a house that will end up becoming yours... there, and you have all of that!”

“What I wanted,” she explained, “was to choose for myself a life different from the one I was leading: nothing else. Perhaps I was mistaken as well.”

He stared at her again with a doubtful look, then changed his line of thought:

“Why are you alone this evening?”

“I am alone many times,” she replied.

They fell silent; a long silence ruled over their uneasiness. He waited for her to speak; she was waiting for his words. And they studied each other attentively; each sought to read the other’s heart.

“So,” he resumed after that pause, “so you have nothing to say to me?”

“Yes, many things... but I am afraid of you.”

“And you are right,” her brother said. “I have reached that hour when nothing and no one is respected any longer, when an entire story is approaching its final peril. Nevertheless, I will listen to you, if you have something to tell me, and I still listen to you with kindness, Lora, because I am still the same... I repeat: still the same.”

And in these last words he put into his voice a tone as tender as a caress.

“Sit down,” he added; “come closer to me.”

“No!” she said twice, “no.”

“Are you afraid?”

She did not answer; but it seemed that anguish, pity, a compassion almost bordering on revulsion, stifled her soul in that refusal.

On the threshold of the half-dark room, Lazzara’s figure appeared, full of hesitation, yet with the air of being there to bring her aid.

The man turned toward her with a sudden movement:

“What do you want?” he lashed out.

The girl did not answer; her frightened eyes moved from one to the other, as if trying to guess.

But Loretta said to her:

“Do not be afraid, Lazzara. Go up to your room and sleep. My brother will leave shortly.”

“Your brother, madam?...” the girl uttered, unable to believe herself in her amazement.

“Go up and sleep, Lazzara,” Lora commanded curtly.

She withdrew in small steps, silent, and disappeared into the darkness. A little later, from within the thickness of the ancient wall, there burst forth the sound of running water, which in the resonance of the night filled the deep house with sound. Then it ceased: the lofty rooms fell asleep.
